passage: Friday, 11:40 pm. Said "bro, that is lit" four times today and nobody blinked, so I guess I sound right now. Suraj's group, six of us, sat on the low wall outside school. Suraj dared us to bunk the last period and ride to the flyover. Everyone said yes in a row, Ankit, then Dev, then me. Only Tanvi said "I have a Maths test" and they laughed, and Tanvi went in. I wanted to say I did not want to, but my mouth said "let's go". We went. I laughed the whole way but my stomach was tight. Everyone knows my new slang. Does anyone know me? — Yash

qa.q: Who dared the group to bunk the last period?
qa.a: Suraj dared them to bunk the last period and ride to the flyover.

qa.q: Why did Yash's mouth say "let's go" when Yash wanted to say no?
qa.a: Yash wanted to belong to Suraj's group; the tight stomach shows the doubt stayed private behind the laughing.

qa.q: What choice at the wall might have kept Yash in the group without going along?
qa.a: Yash could have said "not the bunking, but I am in for the flyover another day", or walked in with Tanvi; a light no with one ally is easier to keep.

qa.q: What might Tanvi have felt when saying "I have a Maths test" and walking in while the others laughed?
qa.a: Tanvi may have felt awkward at being laughed at but steady enough to accept it, giving a calm reason without blaming anyone.

grounding: A teenager takes up the group's slang and goes along with a risky dare to belong, while feeling private doubt and unknown.

passage:
By October, Astrid said “cringe” and “no way, that's so mid” like the others. She had spent her birthday money on the same white trainers Jana and Freja wore, and her mother had only raised an eyebrow.
On Friday the group met at the Malmö harbour. “Everyone jumps off the pier in October,” Jana said. “It's tradition.”
Astrid's stomach turned at the grey water. She laughed and said, “Obviously,” then stood at the back while two boys dared each other. A coastguard boat came by and they all scattered, laughing.
On the bus home, Freja asked, “Wait, do you actually like anything? Like, for yourself?” Astrid didn't know what to answer. Her sketchbook was at the bottom of her bag, unopened for weeks.

qa.q: What did Astrid spend her birthday money on?
qa.a: She spent it on the same white trainers Jana and Freja wore.

qa.q: What was Astrid feeling at the harbour?
qa.a: She felt afraid and doubtful; her stomach turned at the grey water, but she said "Obviously" and hid at the back.

qa.q: What could Astrid do to be known, not just accepted?
qa.a: She could share something real, like her sketchbook, with Freja, and try saying no to things that scare her while staying friendly.

qa.q: How might Freja see Astrid after these weeks?
qa.a: Freja seems to sense that Astrid copies the group but hides herself, and is curious about who she really is.

grounding: Shows a teenager taking up the group's slang, matching shoes and risky dares to belong, while privately doubting and feeling unknown.

passage:
In the boys' hostel at the boarding school, Yogesh's group rolled their sleeves exactly two folds and ended every sentence with “scene hai”. By the second month, Jagdish did too.
“Tonight, after lights-out, we go to the old tank behind the mess,” Yogesh whispered at dinner. “Juniors who come are in.”
Jagdish nodded. Inside, he kept picturing the warden's torch and his father's face if he were sent home.
At eleven he followed them out, sleeves rolled, laughing at jokes he didn't find funny. Nothing happened except mosquitoes. Walking back, Yogesh clapped his shoulder. “You're one of us now.” Jagdish smiled, and wondered why it felt like Yogesh still didn't know a single real thing about him.

qa.q: What did Yogesh's group say at the end of every sentence?
qa.a: They ended every sentence with "scene hai".

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling as he followed the group out?
qa.a: He felt anxious and uneasy; he kept picturing the warden's torch and his father's face, yet went along to be accepted.

qa.q: What could Jagdish try next time the group plans something he doubts?
qa.a: He could stay in, say casually he's tired, and spend time with one of the group one-to-one so they get to know him rather than just his copying.

qa.q: How does Yogesh seem to see Jagdish after that night?
qa.a: Yogesh sees him as properly part of the group now, but only because he followed along, not because he knows him.

grounding: Shows a teenager adopting hostel slang, style and a rule-breaking outing to belong while privately doubtful and not truly known.

passage:
Hi Mohit bhaiya,
Mummy says you're coming for Diwali, so I thought I'd write first. School is okay. I've got a new group, Sid, Nikhil and Faraz. They're funny. I talk like them now, everything is “full bakwaas” or “chill maar”. I even made Papa buy the same black jacket they all have. Papa said it cost more than his.
Last week we bunked tuition and went to the mall. I told Mummy the class was cancelled. I laughed all afternoon, but my stomach hurt the whole time.
The weird thing is, none of them knows I like chess. I haven't mentioned it once.
Can we play when you come?
Raghav

qa.q: Which friends are in Raghav's new group?
qa.a: Sid, Nikhil and Faraz.

qa.q: How can you tell Raghav feels torn about his new group?
qa.a: Raghav says they're funny and laughed all afternoon, but had a stomach ache the whole time and hides a love of chess, which shows guilt and unease.

qa.q: What would you advise Raghav before the next plan to bunk?
qa.a: Raghav could say, "I'll catch you after tuition," and try mentioning chess to one friend to see if they accept the real Raghav.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel reading this email?
qa.a: Mohit might feel touched to be trusted and a bit concerned about the bunking, and glad to be asked to play chess.

grounding: Shows a teenager adopting a new group's slang, jacket and risky bunking to belong while privately doubtful and not truly known.

passage: Samir, you asked why I changed so much in Class 10. Honestly? Aditi was trying to be someone else. The new group said 'bro' about everything, so I said 'bro'. They all wore the same oversized hoodies, so I begged Mummy for one. Then one of the older boys started daring us to ride pillion on his bike without a helmet, fast, down the flyover. Everyone did it. I did it too, once, holding on so tight my fingers hurt, pretending to scream with joy. That night I realised none of them knew I love chemistry, or that I'm scared of speed. They knew my hoodie. I told Mummy about the bike rides that night, and she phoned the class teacher before we slept; the rides stopped that week. I still wear the hoodie sometimes. I don't ride that bike.

qa.q: What did the older boy dare them to do?
qa.a: Ride pillion on his bike without a helmet, fast, down the flyover.

qa.q: What did Aditi realise that night?
qa.a: Aditi felt uneasy and lonely, realising the group knew the hoodie but not the real Aditi, who loves chemistry and fears speed.

qa.q: What protective step followed Aditi telling Mummy?
qa.a: Mummy phoned the class teacher that same night, and the rides stopped that week.

qa.q: How might the others in the group have felt riding the bike?
qa.a: Some may have been as scared as Aditi but hid it too, all pretending to enjoy it in order to belong.

grounding: A teenager takes up a group's slang, clothes and risky dares to belong, while privately doubting it and feeling unknown.
